name: Bullying, Cyberbullying, and Deepfakes
title: Bullying, Cyberbullying, and Deepfakes
answer: Bullying now often happens online, where adults cannot see it, and AI has added fake images and videos of real students as a new form of harm. Schools need ways to learn about online bullying and deepfakes, respond quickly and fairly, and support victims. This idea matters because online harm follows students home, spreads quickly, and can cause serious damage if adults do not act.

sections.body: The idea is that schools must treat online bullying and deepfakes as part of student safety and conduct, not as something outside their reach. Bullying often moves online, where adults cannot see it, and it follows students home and can spread quickly. Anonymous reporting tools give students a way to tell adults what is happening online, and lessons on digital citizenship help them understand the harm of online cruelty and how to respond when they see it. AI has added a new form of harm: fake images and videos of real students, including fake explicit images a student might create with freely available tools. The problem this solves is that schools need ways to learn about online harm and respond, and students report more when they believe something will happen.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the text describes anonymous reporting tools as one way students can tell adults what is happening online, and lessons on digital citizenship help students understand the harm of online cruelty and how to respond when they see it. Adults who respond quickly and fairly to reports build trust that brings more reports, and students report more when they believe something will happen. Schools should include deepfakes in their conduct codes and prepare to support victims. When a deepfake involves a real student, the school should help remove the images, protect the victim from further harm, and connect them with a counselor. The text does not give grade bands for these practices.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites a survey of Chinese middle school students in which more than a third reported involvement in cyberbullying, and students who were both bullies and victims were at the greatest risk of harm (Li et al., 2023). For deepfakes, the text does not cite a study or give an evidence label; it describes the TAKE IT DOWN Act from Chapter 3, which makes knowingly sharing intimate deepfakes a federal crime and requires platforms to remove them quickly. The text does not assign an overall evidence label to this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on how schools should respond. Staff should never share or forward deepfake images, even to report them. Victims of deepfakes need immediate support, and the school should help remove the images, protect the victim from further harm, and connect them with a counselor. Discipline for the student who created the image should follow the district's code, with attention to the serious harm caused. These decisions stay with adults and the school as the text describes them.
